newsitem.title: ROMANIA: FEATURE - ROMANIA TACKLES ISSUE OF LOST JEWISH ASSETS.
newsitem.headline: FEATURE - ROMANIA TACKLES ISSUE OF LOST JEWISH ASSETS.

text.p: Romania, which saw Eastern Europe's biggest post-war exodus of Jews, is getting down to the business of returning to ethnic minorities assets seized first by fascists allied with the Nazis and later by the communists.
Fourteen ethnic groups are seeking restitution, including Hungarians, Germans, Turks and Greeks.
But the Jews' quest is almost certainly the most poignant.
Half of Romania's 800,000 Jews perished in Nazi death camps during World War Two, most rounded up as the Nazis left the region in panic before the Red Army's westward advance.
Of those who survived, 320,000 left communist Romania for Israel and elsewhere. Only 14,000 remain, most of them over 60.
The issue of lost Jewish assets resurfaced when Foreign Minister Teodor Melescanu visited the United States early in October to rally support for Romania's bid for fast-track admission to NATO.
Melescanu met U.S. Jewish leaders, who praised cooperation between Romania's Jewish community and the government.

"Romania is the only East European country which has given unlimited access to minorities to investigate state archives to look for confiscated assets," said Ivan Truter, who heads a government commission on the country's 18 ethnic minorities.
"It's not just the Jewish community property we're considering, but there's greater pressure from the Jews."
The Holocaust and subsequent mass emigration wiped out many Jewish communities from the country.
"There are 785 Jewish cemeteries in Romania. Where there's a cemetery, a community used to exist," said Iulian Sorin, secretary of the Federation of Romanian Jewish communities.
Sorin, who heads a body on restitution representing all ethnic groups, said tracking down lost assets was particularly difficult for Jews.
"A total of 510 Jewish communities no longer exist, there are only cemeteries left," he said. "The work ahead of us is staggering."
Jews were persecuted by members of Romania's Iron Guard, a local fascist movement allied to Hitler's Germany. Jews were barred from office and thrown out of schools in the 1930s.

The wartime Quisling regime of Marshal Ion Antonescu went further in 1941, confiscating Jewish properties under a law on "expropriation of rural, urban and floating assets of the Jews". Floating assets meant boats, Sorin said.
In 1944, hundreds of thousands of Jews were deported to Nazi death camps from areas of Transylvania which had been awarded to Hungary under a 1939 ruling from Hitler.
Elie Wiesel, who won the 1986 Nobel Peace Prize for his writing on the Holocaust, was born there.
Unlike other European countries, Romania pays no damages to Holocaust survivors, saying that is the responsibility of others, like Hungary.
"Jews who returned from camps get some help from local authorities in Hungary," Sorin said. "We don't get any assistance. We have to take care of survivors ourselves."
Moscow-backed communists who took power in Romania after the war did not spare Jews in their drive to nationalise the assets of ethnic or religious groups.
"What the communists gave with one hand, they took back with the other," said Sorin.
A decree issued in December 1944, after Romania switched to the Allied side in the war, repealed the previous anti-Jewish laws and ordered the return of confiscated Jewish properties.
But four years later, the communists took them back again through full-scale nationalisation.
Lost Jewish assets include 295 demolished synagogues and hundreds of expropriated properties -- 165 schools and 31 hospitals as well as ritual baths and homes for the elderly.

The Securitate secret police of executed dictator Nicolae Ceausescu turned a Jewish ritual bath in the main Transylvanian city of Cluj for a time into an Olympic-size swimming pool. The bath is now used as a warehouse.
Carpenters use a former synagogue in Oradea, on the western border with Hungary, as their workshop.

"Ceausescu had several Bucharest synagogues razed. He spared others but deliberately concealed them behind new buildings," Sorin told Reuters from his office near the ornate Choral Temple, dwarfed by a tall, Ceausescu-era apartment bloc.
"The situation is quite complicated," he said. "We can't work within a specific time frame...The (post-communist) government shows goodwill, but it's difficult to count our losses over 50 years."

The 1991 collapse of the Soviet Union had an unpleasant spin-off for East European Jews -- U.S. and other Western Jewish communities channeled aid away from them to Russia and other post-Soviet states whose plight was deemed greater.
"Our ration has been cut due to greater needs in the ex-USSR," said Sorin. His community hoped the return of Jewish assets would provide an alternative source of funding.
"We don't want to throw anybody out," said Sorin. "What we want is to be able to charge the rent owed to us, so that we can assist our sick and elderly."
The whole process requires complicated legislation and will almost certainly be slowed down by presidential and general elections next month.
Drawing up any list will be difficult, given the fast dwindling size of the ageing community.
"It's also difficult to calculate a lump sum for destroyed synagogues which no longer exist," said Sorin. "Some were bigger, others were smaller."
